title: MORSE Boosts Qwen3-VL-8B to 75.1% on OVO-Bench Video Memory
summary: MORSE auto-evolves streaming video memory harnesses, lifting Qwen3-VL-8B to 75.1% on OVO-Bench with 0.30s latency. Research from CMU shows cross-backbone
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- MORSE automates streaming-memory harness design by searching papers and code, lifting frozen Qwen3-VL-8B to 75.1% on OVO-Bench.
- The framework cuts answer latency to 0.30 seconds, roughly 6.0x faster than MemEvo baseline on streaming video queries.
- The evolved harness transfers unchanged to LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B with double-digit accuracy gains.


A frozen Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, wrapped in an automatically evolved memory harness, now answers streaming video queries in 0.30 seconds on average while reaching 75.1% accuracy on OVO-Bench. That represents a 3.1 percentage point gain over the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen model, according to an arxiv preprint from Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang and colleagues at CMU published November 24, 2026.


## What MORSE Does


MORSE is an open-world auto-research framework that automates the design of streaming-memory harnesses by combining recursive self-improvement with online research. The system searches academic papers, model cards and code repositories to adapt new perception tools while leaving the video-language backbone frozen. When training failures recur across videos, the editor groups them by cause and searches for solutions that prior work has already addressed.


The framework introduces new perceptual capabilities by revising how the harness stores and retrieves evidence for the frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance threshold.


## Release Date and Benchmarks


Officially released on November 24, 2026, MORSE delivers 78.9% accuracy on StreamingBench and 71.6% on StreamBench alongside the headline OVO-Bench result. The project page reports roughly 6.0x lower latency compared to a MemEvo baseline, dropping answer times to 0.30 seconds from earlier methods that required multiple seconds per query.


An ablation study on the project page shows research and tool requests both contribute to performance. Removing online research drops the gain to 5.5 points, removing tool requests cuts it to 3.2 points, while the full MORSE configuration achieves a 7.7 point improvement over the frozen backbone alone.


## Cross-Backbone Transfer


The evolved Qwen harness transfers unchanged to other video-language models with significant accuracy gains. LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B sees a 16.3 percentage point lift, while Gemma-4-26B-A4B gains 9.7 points when wrapped in the same memory architecture. These transfer results demonstrate that the harness captures general streaming-video reasoning patterns rather than model-specific optimizations.


The framework groups training failures by cause, enabling it to identify systematic gaps in perception or memory retrieval. When the editor finds a recurring failure pattern, it queries research databases for methods that address similar challenges, then adapts those techniques to the current harness implementation.


## Research Context


MORSE arrives in a visible run of memory-harness work, landing on the same day as MMMem and following recent releases like Future-OPSD on VLM video foresight. The abstract itself publishes only the OVO-Bench headline figure and the 0.30-second latency metric, while StreamingBench, StreamBench and cross-backbone numbers appear on the project page rather than in the archived abstract.


The CMU team structured the framework to maintain a frozen backbone throughout evolution, ensuring that harness improvements come from better memory management and perception tools rather than retraining the underlying video-language model. This design choice enables rapid iteration and deployment without the compute cost of full model fine-tuning.


## What This Means


MORSE demonstrates that automated research and tool integration can close the gap between frozen foundation models and task-specific requirements in streaming video understanding. The 6.0x latency reduction makes real-time video question answering practical for production use cases, while cross-backbone transfer suggests the approach will generalize as new video-language models emerge. Organizations working with long-form video content now have a path to high-accuracy streaming inference without custom model training.
